titulo: update docs for `MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH`
corpo: Clarify [MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH](https://flask.palletsprojects.com/en/stable/config/#MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH) should be avoided in the docs in favor of setting the limit on the server just like [its written in the Werkzeug docs](https://werkzeug.palletsprojects.com/en/stable/request_data/#limiting-request-data).  I have this Flask app with Waitress as the production server and MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH set to 10 bytes ```python from flask import Flask,request from waitress import serve  app=Flask(__name__) app.config["MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH"]=10  @app.post("/") def index():     print(request.get_data())     return "OK"  serve(app,listen="localhost:8000") ``` and this client to send data to it until the connection is closed ```python from urllib.request import urlopen from random import randbytes  bytes_sent=0 chunk_size=10_000_000 def stream():     global bytes_sent      while True:         yield randbytes(chunk_size)         bytes_sent+=chunk_size  try:     urlopen("http://localhost:8000/",stream()) except Exception as e:     print(e) print(f"sent around {bytes_sent} bytes") ``` and the app kept receiving and writing the request to disk way over 10 bytes until it hit Waitress's max_request_body_size limit that defaults to 1Gib, with the client printing ``` <urlopen error [WinError 10054] ...> sent around 1080000000 bytes ```  Environment:  - Python version: 3.13.7 - Flask version: 3.1.3

titulo: `add_url_rule` leaves a route registered even after an endpoint conflict
corpo: ## Description ‘add_url_rule’ correctly raises an error when an endpoint already exists and you try to register a different view function with the same endpoint.  However, after you catch the error and continue running the code, the URL you tried to add (/b, for example) still exists. When a user requests /b, it is routed to the view function that was already registered for that endpoint, rather than the new view function whose registration failed.  ## Example  ```python from flask import Flask  app = Flask(__name__)  def first():     return "first"  def second():     return "second"  app.add_url_rule("/a", endpoint="same", view_func=first)  try:     app.add_url_rule("/b", endpoint="same", view_func=second) except AssertionError as e:     print(e)  client = app.test_client()  print(client.get("/a").status_code, client.get("/a").data) print(client.get("/b").status_code, client.get("/b").data) ```  ### Expected Result  ```text View function mapping is overwriting an existing endpoint function: same 200 b'first' 404 ... ```  ### Actual Result  ```text View function mapping is overwriting an existing endpoint function: same 200 b'first' 200 b'first' ```  I think Flask correctly rejects the view-function overwrite, but the failed registration has already added the URL rule.  Environment:  - Python version: 3.11.2 - Flask version: 3.1.3

titulo: `stream_with_context`: abandoned generator leaves the app context current on the worker thread; later requests skip `teardown_appcontext`
corpo: `stream_with_context` pushes the request's contexts onto whichever thread iterates the response body, and pops them only if the generator completes or is closed on that same thread. When a client disconnects mid-stream, the server abandons the body iterator and GC finalizes it later — often on a different thread. That cross-context pop fails (`LookupError`/`ValueError` from `ContextVar.reset`, swallowed as "Exception ignored in ..."), and the app context stays current on the worker thread.  Because `RequestContext.push` reuses an ambient app context of the same app, every later request on that pooled thread runs under the stuck context and `teardown_appcontext` never fires for it. Anything keyed to the app context then leaks once per thread for the life of the process — with Flask-SQLAlchemy that is one connection held idle-in-transaction per poisoned thread, with nothing in the logs.  Related: #5774 fixed the same cross-context token failure for async views; #5804 covers teardown ordering in the 3.1.2 rewrite. Neither covers the abandonment case. The docs mention that headers/session need care with `stream_with_context`, but not that a disconnect can leave the context stuck on the thread — a warning there would be helpful even if the behavior itself is hard to change.  ## Reproduction  One long-lived "worker" thread serves two requests; the abandoned body iterator is GC-finalized on the main thread in between (in real deployments the reference is dropped by server machinery outside the worker — servers may never call `close()` on the iterator after a disconnect):  ```python import gc import queue import threading  from flask import Flask, Response, stream_with_context from flask.globals import _cv_app  app = Flask(__name__) teardowns = []  @app.teardown_appcontext def note_teardown(exc):     teardowns.append(threading.current_thread().name)  @app.route("/stream") def stream():     def gen():         for i in range(100):             yield f"chunk{i}\n"     return Response(stream_with_context(gen()))  @app.route("/plain") def plain():     return "ok"  abandoned = queue.Queue()   # holds the dropped iterator, like server machinery step2 = threading.Event()  def worker():     # --- request A: streaming response, client disconnects after one chunk ---     with app.test_request_context("/stream"):         rv = app.full_dispatch_request()     body = iter(rv.response)     next(body)   # first chunk: stream_with_context pushes app+request ctx HERE     abandoned.put((body, rv))   # server-side reference outlives the request     del body, rv     print("A: ambient ctx after abandonment:", _cv_app.get(None))      step2.wait()  # main thread GC-finalizes the generator meanwhile      # --- request B: any later request on this pooled worker thread ---     print("B: ambient ctx at request start:", _cv_app.get(None))     teardowns.clear()     with app.test_request_context("/plain"):    # reuses the ambient ctx of the         app.full_dispatch_request()             # same app -> no fresh app ctx     print("B: teardown_appcontext ran for B:", bool(teardowns))     print("B: ambient ctx after B finished:", _cv_app.get(None))  t = threading.Thread(target=worker, name="wsgi-worker-0") t.start()  abandoned.get()          # take the reference, then drop it on the MAIN thread gc.collect()             # generator finalized here -> cross-context pop fails step2.set() t.join() ```  Output (Flask 3.1.3, Python 3.13):  ``` Exception ignored in: <generator object stream_with_context.<locals>.generator at 0x...> Traceback (most recent call last):   File ".../flask/helpers.py", line 130, in generator     with app_ctx, req_ctx:   File ".../flask/ctx.py", line 284, in __exit__     self.pop(exc_value)   File ".../flask/ctx.py", line 264, in pop     ctx = _cv_app.get() LookupError: <ContextVar name='flask.app_ctx' at 0x...> A: ambient ctx after abandonment: <flask.ctx.AppContext object at 0x10b49c830> B: ambient ctx at request start: <flask.ctx.AppContext object at 0x10b49c830> B: teardown_appcontext ran for B: False B: ambient ctx after B finished: <flask.ctx.AppContext object at 0x10b49c830> ```  ## Expected behavior  Request B runs under its own app context and `teardown_appcontext` fires when it finishes. Instead it silently runs under request A's leaked context, teardown never runs, and the thread stays poisoned indefinitely.  Environment:  - Python version: 3.13 (also reproduced on 3.11) - Flask version: 3.1.3. The `main` branch (3.2-dev, post-#5639 merged context) looks affected as well: `stream_with_context` there enters the single context via `with ctx:` around the priming `yield None`, so the context is pushed at creation and only exited when the generator completes or is closed.

corpo: ## Summary  `Config.from_prefixed_env` can raise an uncaught `TypeError` when an environment variable creates a scalar configuration value and another variable later tries to use that same value as a nested mapping.  ### Reproduction  With Flask's development source at commit `6a2f545bfd8ed31e19066a299296917e034aca58`:  ```bash FLASK_FOO=bar FLASK_FOO__BAR=baz python - <<'PY' from flask import Flask  app = Flask(__name__) app.config.from_prefixed_env() PY ```  The call raises:  ```text TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment ```  ### What happens  `from_prefixed_env` processes matching environment variables in sorted order. The first variable sets `config["FOO"]` to the string `"bar"`. When processing `FLASK_FOO__BAR`, the nested traversal reaches this value and then attempts to assign through it:  ```python current = current[part] ... current[tail] = value ```  The intermediate value is a string rather than a mapping, so configuration loading fails with a low-level `TypeError`.  Relevant source at the reproduction commit: <https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/6a2f545bfd8ed31e19066a299296917e034aca58/src/flask/config.py#L172-L183>  ### Expected behavior  Configuration loading should not fail with an implementation-level `TypeError` for a prefix collision. The behavior should be defined and deterministic, for example by rejecting the conflicting configuration with a clear error, or by documenting and implementing precedence/merge semantics.  ### Impact  An application can fail during startup or configuration initialization when environment variables are assembled from multiple sources and a scalar key and nested key happen to share a prefix. This can be difficult to diagnose because the error does not identify the conflicting environment variables.  ### Suggested regression test  Add a test covering both `FLASK_FOO=bar` and `FLASK_FOO__BAR=baz`, and assert the chosen behavior for the scalar/nested conflict. If the intended behavior is to reject the configuration, the error should identify the conflicting path.  ### Environment  - Flask source commit: `6a2f545bfd8ed31e19066a299296917e034aca58` - Flask version: `3.2.0.dev` - Python: `3.13.13` - Reproduction is independent of operating system semantics because it only   relies on the environment-variable traversal logic.  I have not assigned a CWE classification. This is reported as a configuration robustness and error-handling issue rather than a nullability finding.

titulo: jsonify emits NaN and Infinity, which are not valid JSON
corpo: `jsonify` serialises `float("nan")` and `float("inf")` as the bare literals `NaN` and `Infinity`. Those are not valid JSON (RFC 8259 allows only decimal numbers), so the response is served as `application/json` but cannot be parsed by a strict parser, including the browser's `JSON.parse`.  This inherits from `json.dumps`, whose `allow_nan` defaults to `True`. `DefaultJSONProvider` sets `default`, `ensure_ascii` and `sort_keys`, but never touches `allow_nan`, so the permissive default applies.  The path to it is ordinary: any average, ratio or division that can meet an empty input produces `nan` without anything looking wrong on the server.  Replication:  ```python from flask import Flask, jsonify  app = Flask(__name__)  @app.route("/stats") def stats():     values = []     mean = sum(values) / len(values) if values else float("nan")     return jsonify({"count": len(values), "mean": mean})  with app.test_client() as c:     r = c.get("/stats")     print(r.headers["Content-Type"])      # application/json     print(r.get_data(as_text=True))       # {"count":0,"mean":NaN} ```  The response advertises `application/json` with a 200, but the body is not JSON:  ```python import json json.loads('{"count":0,"mean":NaN}')      # accepted, Python is permissive by default json.loads('{"count":0,"mean":NaN}',            parse_constant=lambda x: (_ for _ in ()).throw(ValueError(x))) # ValueError: NaN     <- what a strict parser, and JSON.parse in a browser, does ```  So the failure surfaces in the client rather than the server, which makes it awkward to trace back.  Expected: either the same behaviour with it documented, or serialisation raises so the problem shows up server-side, where `ValueError: Out of range float values are not JSON compliant: nan` names the cause immediately.  There is currently no class attribute for this, although the plumbing already works, since `dumps` forwards `**kwargs` to `json.dumps`:  ```python app.json.dumps({"a": float("nan")}, allow_nan=False) # ValueError: Out of range float values are not JSON compliant: nan ```  `DefaultJSONProvider` exposes `sort_keys`, `ensure_ascii` and `compact` as class attributes, so an `allow_nan` attribute alongside them would fit the existing pattern and let applications choose, without changing the default for anyone. I could not find `NaN` mentioned in the `DefaultJSONProvider` or `flask.json.dumps` docstrings, so at minimum a documentation note seems worthwhile.  Happy to send a PR for whichever you prefer, an `allow_nan` provider attribute or just the docs.  Environment:  - Python 3.14 - Flask 3.1.3 - Werkzeug 3.1.8

titulo: Confusing docstring in Flask.get_send_file_max_age and Flask.send_static_file
corpo: This is a documentation issue rather than a functional bug. titulo: Tests fail with pytest 9.1: _pytest.monkeypatch.notset removed
corpo: Flask's test suite imports the private notset sentinel from _pytest.monkeypatch in both tests/conftest.py and tests/test_cli.py. pytest 9.1 removed this attribute, moving it to _pytest.compat.NOTSET. titulo: Add a query() route shortcut and MethodView support for HTTP QUERY (RFC 10008)
corpo: The HTTP `QUERY` method was standardized in [RFC 10008](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc10008/) (June 2026): a safe, idempotent request method that carries content in the request body (the standardized replacement for the "use POST for a read-only query with a large body" workaround in GraphQL / REST search APIs).  I'd like Flask to treat `QUERY` as a first-class method like the others:  - a `query()` route shortcut on `Scaffold` (inherited by `Flask` and   `Blueprint`), mirroring `get`/`post`/`put`/`delete`/`patch`; - `MethodView` dispatch of `QUERY` to a `query` handler (add `"query"` to   `views.http_method_funcs`).  ---  Is this solvable without changes to Flask? Partly — `@app.route("/x", methods=["QUERY"])` already works today, since Flask doesn't restrict method names and Werkzeug parses the body. What's missing is the ergonomic shortcut and `MethodView` dispatch that every other common method already has, so this is a consistency/ergonomics gap rather than new capability — the same rationale behind the existing `get`/`post`/... shortcuts. Use case: safe, idempotent search endpoints that need a request body too large or complex for the URL.

titulo: register_blueprint name override bypasses dot validation
corpo: The `Blueprint` constructor explicitly prevents dots in names (`if "." in name: raise ValueError`) because dots denote nested blueprints. However, `app.register_blueprint(..., name="...")` doesn't enforce this check on the overridden name.  If a blueprint is registered with a dot via the `name` kwarg, it bypasses the restriction. This tricks the framework into treating it as a nested blueprint, causing the parent's callbacks (like `before_request`) to unexpectedly execute for the unrelated child blueprint.  ### How to replicate the bug ```python import flask  app = flask.Flask(__name__) parent = flask.Blueprint("parent", __name__) child = flask.Blueprint("child", __name__)  parent.before_request(lambda: setattr(flask.g, "hit", True)) child.add_url_rule("/", "index", lambda: str(hasattr(flask.g, "hit")))  app.register_blueprint(parent) app.register_blueprint(child, name="parent.fake") # Bypasses dot validation  print(app.test_client().get("/").get_data(as_text=True))

titulo: multiple teardown errors are discarded on Python < 3.11
corpo: Markdown On Python versions prior to 3.11, `_CollectErrors.raise_any()` (in `src/flask/helpers.py`, line 682) only re-raises the very first collected error, silently swallowing any subsequent teardown errors. This makes debugging secondary teardown failures impossible on Python < 3.11.  ### How to replicate the bug 1. Create a `_CollectErrors` context manager. 2. Trigger multiple teardown exceptions (e.g., DB close fails, then Cache flush fails). 3. Call `raise_any()`. Only the first exception is raised; the others are silently lost.  **Minimal Reproducible Example:** ```python import sys  class _CollectErrors:     def __init__(self):         self.errors = []      def __enter__(self):         pass      def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb):         if exc_val is not None:             self.errors.append(exc_val)         return True      def raise_any(self, message: str) -> None:         if self.errors:             if sys.version_info >= (3, 11):                 raise BaseExceptionGroup(message, self.errors)             else:                 raise self.errors[0]   # BUG: only first error raised  collect = _CollectErrors()  with collect:     raise RuntimeError("DB connection close failed") with collect:     raise ValueError("File handle close failed")  try:     collect.raise_any("Teardown errors") except Exception as e:     print(f"Raised: {type(e).__name__}: {e}")     print(f"Total collected: {len(collect.errors)}") ```  Expected behavior Even without BaseExceptionGroup (which is 3.11+), subsequent errors should not be silently discarded. They should ideally be chained or at least logged before raising the first error.  Proposed Fix Consider chaining the exceptions or logging the secondary ones before raising the first on Python versions < 3.11.  Environment:  Python version: < 3.11 (e.g., 3.10)  Flask version: 3.2.0.dev (flask-main branch)

titulo: Config.from_file() silently ignores fewer OSError codes than from_pyfile()
corpo: ## Summary  `Config.from_file()` and `Config.from_pyfile()` behave inconsistently when `silent=True` and an `OSError` is raised.  `from_pyfile()` silences errors for these `errno` codes:  ```python if silent and e.errno in (errno.ENOENT, errno.EISDIR, errno.ENOTDIR):     return False ```  But `from_file()` only silences:  ```python if silent and e.errno in (errno.ENOENT, errno.EISDIR):     return False ```  It is missing `errno.ENOTDIR`.  ## Reproduction  `ENOTDIR` is raised when a path component is a regular file, not a directory. For example, if `/tmp/myconfig` is a regular file and you try to open `/tmp/myconfig/settings.json`, the OS raises `ENOTDIR` (not a directory).  ```python import os, tempfile from flask import Flask  app = Flask(__name__)  # create a file where we expect a directory with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(delete=False, suffix="cfg") as f:     f.write(b"")     tmp = f.name  # from_pyfile with silent=True returns False (correct) result = app.config.from_pyfile(tmp + "/nested.cfg", silent=True) # from_file with silent=True raises OSError instead of returning False (bug) result = app.config.from_file(tmp + "/nested.json", load=json.load, silent=True) ```  ## Expected behavior  Both methods should return `False` when `silent=True` and the path is not reachable due to `ENOTDIR`, just like they both return `False` for `ENOENT` and `EISDIR`.  ## Fix  Add `errno.ENOTDIR` to the tuple in `from_file()`:  ```python if silent and e.errno in (errno.ENOENT, errno.EISDIR, errno.ENOTDIR):     return False ```

titulo: Add a built-in is_safe_redirect() helper to handle browser URL normalization (backslash → forward slash)
corpo: Modern browsers normalize backslashes in navigation URLs (e.g., `\\evil.com`) into forward slashes (`//evil.com`). This creates a discrepancy between how Flask/Werkzeug evaluates redirect targets and how user agents ultimately interpret them.  A common pattern used by Flask developers to prevent protocol-relative redirects is:  ```python if not url.startswith("//"):     return redirect(url) ```  However, the following payload bypasses this logic:  ``` \\evil.com ```  Flask/Werkzeug evaluates this as a safe relative path (`startswith("//") == False`), while browsers normalize it to:  ``` https://evil.com ```  and perform an external redirect. This normalization behavior is consistent across Chrome, Firefox, and Safari.  As Flask does not provide a built-in redirect validation helper, developers routinely implement ad-hoc string checks that do not account for browser normalization rules, resulting in an ecosystem-wide class of open-redirect flaws.  **Feature Request**  Introduce an official, browser-aware redirect safety utility in Flask or Werkzeug, similar to Django’s `is_safe_url`, to standardize redirect validation across the framework. The helper should:  1. Normalize backslashes to forward slashes before validation. 2. Reject protocol-relative URLs (`//example.com`). 3. Optionally enforce allowed host checks. 4. Provide a documented, recommended pattern for safe redirects.  **Rationale**  - This issue is not a flaw in Flask’s redirect implementation but a recurring security footgun for developers due to inconsistent handling between application logic and browser URL normalization. - Providing an official helper reduces the likelihood of open-redirect vulnerabilities in applications built on Flask. - This is framework hardening rather than a security bug report, and it aligns with the expectations set by other frameworks that offer standardized redirect-safety utilities.  This feature would give developers a reliable and recommended approach to validating redirect targets securely, reducing reliance on fragile custom logic.

titulo: Add configurable JSON parsing limits and preprocessing hook
corpo: Description Flask currently parses JSON input using json.loads() without providing an application-level mechanism to enforce payload size limits or preprocess raw JSON before deserialization. This feature would introduce configuration settings such as: •⁠  ⁠JSON_MAX_STRING_LENGTH – to reject JSON payloads exceeding a defined size before parsing. •⁠  ⁠JSON_PREPROCESS_RAW – to allow an optional callable to preprocess raw JSON text before json.loads() is executed.  Example of the Problem This Would Resolve If a client sends a very large JSON payload (for example, 15–20MB), Flask will attempt to parse it entirely in memory. This can lead to unnecessary memory consumption and CPU usage, especially in API-heavy environments. While infrastructure-level limits (e.g., reverse proxies) may mitigate this, application-level safeguards provide defense-in-depth and improve reliability. Currently, this problem can only be addressed by subclassing JSONProvider, overriding loads(), or modifying framework internals. Providing built-in configuration support would make it easier to enforce consistent JSON parsing policies without custom framework patches.
